title: Debt Snowball
description: A step-by-step way to pay off debt: smallest balance first, then roll the payment forward.

lessons.title: What is the debt snowball?
body: The debt snowball is a plan for paying off several debts. You attack the smallest balance first, no matter the interest rate.
When that debt is gone, its payment "rolls" onto the next one. Each payment gets bigger, like a snowball rolling downhill.
Why smallest first? Quick wins. Seeing a debt hit $0 in a few months keeps you motivated, and motivation is what gets people all the way to debt-free.
lessons.keyIdea: Smallest starting balance first. Roll each paid-off payment into the next debt.
lessons.example: You owe $300, $800, and $4,000. You throw every extra dollar at the $300 debt first.

lessons.title: The 5 steps
body: 1. List every debt with its balance, minimum payment, and APR.
2. Sort them from smallest balance to largest, using each debt's starting balance. That order is set once at the start; you don't re-sort every month.
3. Pay the minimum on every debt, every month. (Missing payments hurts your credit and adds fees.)
4. Put every extra dollar you can find on the smallest debt.
5. When it's paid off, add its old payment to the next debt's payment. Repeat until you're debt-free! 🎉
lessons.keyIdea: Your total monthly debt payment never shrinks. It just moves to the next target.
lessons.example: Find extra money by trimming wants, selling stuff you don't use, or picking up extra shifts.

lessons.title: A worked example
body: Here are three debts and $100 a month extra. Every number below is calculated live by the same math as the Snowball calculator.
lessons.keyIdea: Watch how the payment on each target grows as earlier debts disappear.
lessons.example: Open the Snowball calculator and press "Load example" to see the month-by-month table.

lessons.title: Snowball vs. avalanche
body: The avalanche method targets the highest APR first instead of the smallest balance.
Avalanche usually saves some interest, because the most expensive debt goes first. Snowball usually gives you your first win sooner.
In the worked example, avalanche saves about $27 in interest, and both finish in the same month. The best plan is the one you'll actually stick with.
lessons.keyIdea: Snowball = smallest balance first (motivation). Avalanche = highest APR first (math).
lessons.example: If one debt has a huge APR (like 29%) and a big balance, avalanche can save a lot. Try both in the calculator.

lessons.title: Don't refill the bucket
body: Paying off debt only works if you stop adding new debt. Put the credit card away (or use it only for things you pay in full).
Build a small emergency fund ($500 to $1,000) first, so a surprise bill doesn't go back on a card.
When you're debt-free, keep making the same total payment, but to yourself: savings, a car fund, or investing.
lessons.keyIdea: Starter emergency fund → snowball the debts → save the payment you used to make.
lessons.example: Once the debts above are gone, that $305 a month could go to savings. In one year that's $3,660.

practice.prompt: You owe: Credit card $1,200 (22% APR), Medical bill $250 (0%), Car loan $5,000 (7%). Using the snowball, which do you pay off first?
practice.explanation: Snowball goes by smallest balance, not interest rate. The $250 medical bill is first.
practice.reviewed: Ordering question; the smallest balance is read off the list.

practice.prompt: Same debts. Using the avalanche, which do you pay off first?
practice.explanation: Avalanche goes by highest APR. The 22% credit card is first.

practice.prompt: You were paying $25 minimum + $100 extra on a debt that's now paid off. The next debt's minimum is $30. How much do you pay on it now each month?
practice.explanation: Its own $30 minimum + the old $25 minimum + the $100 extra = $155 a month. That's the snowball growing.

practice.prompt: In the worked example (Phone $300, Store card $800, Car loan $4,000, $100 extra), how many months until you're debt-free with the snowball?
practice.explanation: The phone is gone in month 3, the store card in month 8, and the car loan in month 18.

practice.prompt: What should you pay on the debts that aren't your current target?
choices: At least the minimum payment, every month
Whatever is left at the end of the month
practice.explanation: Always pay every minimum. Skipping causes late fees, more interest, and credit score damage.

quiz.prompt: The debt snowball pays off debts in what order?
quiz.explanation: Smallest balance first, for quick wins.

quiz.prompt: What is the main reason people like the snowball method?
choices: It always saves the most interest
quiz.explanation: Paying off a whole debt quickly feels great, and that motivation keeps people going. (Avalanche usually saves more interest.)

quiz.prompt: Debts: Store card $800 (24% APR, $30 min), Car loan $4,000 (6%, $150 min), Phone $300 (0%, $25 min). With $100 extra per month, about how much total interest does the snowball cost?
quiz.explanation: About $306 in interest. Avalanche would cost about $279 for the same debts.

quiz.prompt: Same debts, but using the avalanche method. About how much total interest?
quiz.explanation: About $279, roughly $27 less than the snowball, because the 24% card goes first.

quiz.prompt: Debt A is paid off. You were paying $40 minimum + $60 extra on it. Debt B's minimum is $50. What do you pay on Debt B now?
With the same three debts and $100 extra, what happens if you only pay the minimums with no extra and no rollover?
choices: You finish in 18 months, same as the snowball
It takes 39 months and costs more than twice the interest
quiz.explanation: Minimums only pays $205 a month instead of $305, so it takes 39 months and about $659 interest. The snowball: 18 months and about $306.

quiz.prompt: What should you do before starting the snowball?
choices: Save a small emergency fund so surprises don't go on a card
quiz.explanation: A $500–$1,000 starter emergency fund keeps new surprises from becoming new debt.

flashcards.back: Pay minimums on all debts; put extra on the smallest balance; roll each paid-off payment into the next.
Same idea, but target the highest APR first. Usually saves more interest.
When a debt is paid off, its payment moves to the next debt instead of disappearing.
The month your last debt hits $0.
The least you must pay each month. Always pay it on every debt.
